How to Start a Hair Salon in 2027: Costs, Checklist & Business Plan

Opening your own hair salon can be an exciting opportunity to turn professional skills and entrepreneurial ambition into a business.

But starting a successful salon involves much more than finding a location and purchasing styling chairs.

You need a realistic budget, a clear business model, appropriate licenses, reliable employees, effective marketing, and a system for managing appointments and daily operations.

This guide explains how to start a hair salon step by step, including startup costs, business planning, equipment, staffing, and common mistakes to avoid.

1. Choose Your Salon Business Model

Before making financial commitments, decide what type of salon you want to operate.

Common models include:

Independent hair salon

A traditional salon offering haircuts, coloring, styling, and related services.

Salon suite

A smaller private space operated by an independent beauty professional.

Chair-rental salon

A business where independent professionals rent workspace, subject to applicable local laws and contractual arrangements.

Premium salon

A salon positioned around specialized services, an elevated customer experience, or higher-end products.

Multi-service beauty salon

A business combining hair services with additional beauty treatments.

Your business model influences startup costs, staffing needs, legal requirements, and pricing.

2. Research Your Local Market

Before signing a lease, investigate the area where you want to operate.

Consider:

  • Local population and demographics

  • Nearby competitors

  • Typical service prices

  • Parking and accessibility

  • Pedestrian activity

  • Commercial rent

  • Customer preferences

  • Demand for specific services

Visit competing salons as a prospective customer when appropriate, review their public service menus, and evaluate their positioning.

The goal isn't to copy competitors.

It's to identify opportunities to serve customers better or offer a differentiated experience.

3. Estimate Hair Salon Startup Costs

Startup costs vary significantly by location, salon size, condition of the premises, equipment quality, and regulatory requirements.

For illustration, consider the following planning budget for a small salon in the United States.

A home-based studio, salon suite, or larger commercial salon could have a substantially different budget.

Request local estimates before making investment decisions.

4. Create a Salon Business Plan

A business plan helps you evaluate whether your salon can become financially sustainable.

Include the following sections:

Business overview

Describe your salon concept, target customers, location, and services.

Market analysis

Explain local demand, competitors, and your competitive advantage.

Service menu

List services, expected durations, and planned prices.

Marketing strategy

Explain how customers will discover and book your salon.

Operations plan

Describe staffing, working hours, booking processes, and daily responsibilities.

Financial projections

Estimate startup costs, monthly expenses, expected revenue, and cash requirements.

Your plan should be realistic rather than based on optimistic assumptions.

5. Understand Licenses and Legal Requirements

Salon licensing rules vary by jurisdiction.

In the United States, requirements can differ by state and municipality. In Canada, they can vary by province and local authority.

Depending on your location and business model, you may need:

  • Business registration

  • Salon establishment licenses

  • Individual professional licenses

  • Building or occupancy approvals

  • Health and sanitation compliance

  • Sales tax or other tax registrations

  • Employer registrations

  • Business insurance

Contact the relevant government and professional licensing authorities before opening.

Do not assume that a license from one jurisdiction is valid in another.

6. Find the Right Salon Location

Location can influence visibility, operating costs, and customer convenience.

Evaluate:

  • Accessibility

  • Parking

  • Public transportation

  • Surrounding businesses

  • Rent and lease terms

  • Available utilities

  • Plumbing and electrical capacity

  • Space for styling and washing stations

A cheaper location isn't always the best option if customers find it difficult to reach.

Before signing a lease, verify that the premises can legally and practically support your intended salon services.

7. Purchase Essential Equipment

Your equipment requirements will depend on your service menu.

Common salon essentials include:

  • Styling chairs

  • Mirrors

  • Shampoo stations

  • Hair dryers

  • Clippers and scissors

  • Styling tools

  • Storage cabinets

  • Reception furniture

  • Cleaning and sanitation supplies

  • Towels and protective capes

  • Appropriate lighting

Prioritize equipment that supports safety, service quality, and daily efficiency.

Avoid spending excessively on decorative features before securing essential operating equipment and working capital.

8. Hire and Organize Your Team

If you plan to hire employees, define responsibilities before recruitment.

Potential roles include:

  • Hairstylists

  • Color specialists

  • Salon assistants

  • Reception staff

  • Salon manager

Consider how each role contributes to customer service and revenue.

Establish clear working hours, service responsibilities, compensation arrangements, and training expectations.

Comply with applicable employment, licensing, and worker-classification requirements.

9. Set Profitable Service Prices

Pricing should account for more than the cost of products used during an appointment.

Consider:

  • Staff compensation

  • Rent

  • Utilities

  • Product costs

  • Equipment maintenance

  • Insurance

  • Payment processing

  • Marketing

  • Business taxes

  • Desired profit

For example, a $60 haircut isn't necessarily more profitable than a $45 haircut if it requires significantly more time and expense.

Evaluate each service based on both its contribution margin and the time required to deliver it.

10. Calculate Your Break-Even Point

Understanding your break-even point helps you estimate the number of appointments needed to cover expenses.

Suppose your salon has:

  • Monthly fixed expenses: $8,000

  • Average appointment revenue: $65

  • Average variable cost per appointment: $15

Contribution per appointment:

$65 − $15 = $50

Break-even appointments:

$8,000 ÷ $50 = 160 appointments per month.

If your salon operates 25 days each month, that represents approximately 6.4 completed appointments per operating day.

This simplified example excludes certain taxes, financing costs, and other potential expenses. It assumes that the $8,000 fixed-cost figure includes all applicable fixed compensation and overhead.

11. Create Your Website and Online Booking Experience

Before opening, establish a professional online presence.

Your website should include:

  • Salon name and branding

  • Services and prices

  • Business location

  • Opening hours

  • Contact information

  • Authentic salon photos

  • Booking instructions

Make it easy for customers to schedule appointments from their phones.

Your booking experience should be ready before you begin promoting your salon.

12. Choose Salon Management Software

As appointments increase, manual scheduling can become difficult.

Salon management software can help organize your business from the beginning.

Look for a platform that supports:

  • Appointment booking

  • Service configuration

  • Team management

  • Staff availability

  • Location information

  • Organized booking calendars

Explore https://clipperdesk.com to learn how you can organize your salon's daily operations.

13. Plan Your Salon Launch

Start promoting your salon before opening day.

Consider:

  • Creating a Google Business Profile

  • Launching your website

  • Sharing progress on social media

  • Introducing your team

  • Photographing your completed salon

  • Building relationships with neighboring businesses

  • Offering an appropriate introductory promotion

Make sure advertised opening dates and services are accurate.

A successful launch depends on both marketing and operational readiness.

14. Avoid Common Salon Startup Mistakes

New salon owners sometimes underestimate the challenges of running a service business.

Common mistakes include:

Underestimating startup expenses

Keep a financial contingency and adequate working capital.

Choosing a location based only on rent

Evaluate accessibility, suitability, and customer demand.

Setting prices without understanding costs

Calculate service margins before finalizing prices.

Hiring without clear processes

Define responsibilities and scheduling procedures early.

Neglecting customer experience

A beautiful salon cannot compensate for unreliable appointments or poor service.

Ignoring digital booking

Make it convenient for customers to find and schedule your services.

Hair Salon Opening Checklist

Before welcoming your first customer, review the following:

  • Choose your salon business model

  • Research local competition

  • Prepare a business plan

  • Estimate startup and operating costs

  • Secure appropriate financing

  • Verify licenses and permits

  • Select a suitable location

  • Complete necessary renovations

  • Purchase essential equipment

  • Establish supplier relationships

  • Recruit and train staff

  • Finalize services and prices

  • Create your website

  • Configure online booking

  • Prepare your marketing launch

  • Test the customer appointment experience

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does it cost to start a hair salon?

Costs depend heavily on location, salon size, renovations, and equipment. Build a location-specific budget rather than relying on a single national estimate.

Can I open a salon without being a licensed hairstylist?

Ownership and professional licensing requirements differ by jurisdiction. Some locations distinguish business ownership from performing regulated services. Verify local rules before investing.

How do I attract my first salon customers?

Begin with local online visibility, authentic photographs, referrals, partnerships, clear service information, and convenient appointment booking.

What software does a new salon need?

At minimum, consider tools for appointment scheduling, service management, staff coordination, and essential business records.

How long does it take to open a salon?

The timeline depends on property readiness, licensing, renovations, financing, and staffing. Create a project schedule based on local requirements rather than assuming a fixed opening period.

Final Thoughts

Opening a salon is both a creative opportunity and a serious business commitment.

Careful financial planning, a suitable location, a clear service menu, and efficient operations can help establish a stronger foundation.

Start with a realistic plan, focus on customer experience, and choose systems that support your future growth.
